transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-06-04 08:00 PT / 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Alex Mercer (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (CTO - Oakridge), Samir Patel (Head of ML - Oakridge), Jordan Lee (Platform Eng)

Summary (auto): quick QBR, highlight cost spikes, pipeline for Dedicated pilot, security checklist ask.

[00:00] Alex Mercer: ok good morning everyone, um thanks for carving out time for the QBR, Maya thanks for kicking us off if you want
[00:18] Maya Chen: yeah sure, thanks Alex. quick context, we had a big spike during the last promo week, costs went up by about 2.6x and latency hit the P95 around 420 ms which is... not great for checkout flow
[00:34] Samir Patel: and just to add, our production traces show KV cache hits dipped when concurrency spiked, we think prefix cache warming wasn't happening, so some of the token regen cost was higher
[00:50] Priya Shah: okay, got it. when you say KV cache are you referring to the K V cache on the Redwood runtime, or do you mean your side cache?
[01:02] Jordan Lee: it's mostly on Redwood side, we saw longer cold-starts on the kv-store, we haven't instrumented fully but traces point to model variant swap during the surge
[01:18] Alex Mercer: yeah and to be clear there was a moment we fell back to a cheaper variant to keep throughput - that probably lengthened tail latency, that's our failover policy in action
[01:34] Maya Chen: right which is ok but we need a consistent P95 under 250 ms for checkout, otherwise conversion drops
[01:48] Priya Shah: under 250 P95 for checkout, noted. do you have traffic profile sample to share? burstiness, qps distribution?
[01:58] Samir Patel: yes we'll share. we have the holiday promo windows: 14:00-18:00 UTC, usually 3-4x baseline. overall 30 minute spikes sometimes
[02:12] Alex Mercer: great, that helps. on cost side we looked at the last 90 days and built a couple scenarios - free tier hosted vs committed dedicated. I'll walk through the model in a sec
[02:24] [02:24] Speaker 1: (paper rustling)
[02:30] Alex Mercer: ok slide-free: hosted gives fastest time-to-market, but unit token cost increases under sustained spikes; dedicated gives predictable throughput and lower unit cost but needs a commit level
[02:46] Maya Chen: the finance team really needs predictability; they asked 'how much commit to avoid bill shocks for a 3x promo'
[02:58] Priya Shah: we ran simulations using your traffic numbers and a 2x committed tier covers 80% of incidents but we'd need at least 3x to hit the P95 target consistently with current model sizes
[03:16] Jordan Lee: what are our lever options? batching, quantization, or smaller model variants?
[03:26] Priya Shah: yep all of the above. batching helps throughput but increases per-request latency; quantization can reduce GPU memory and cost but may slightly degrade output quality; also model routing to smaller variants for non-critical requests helps
[03:42] Samir Patel: we can't degrade checkout quality; there's fraud detection prompts attached, so quality is a hard constraint
[03:50] Alex Mercer: understood, so our recommendation: -- dedicated pilot pinning current model with autoscale headroom for 3x burst, plus prefix cache warmers pre-seed before promo windows, and a separate route for non-critical background traffic
[04:08] Maya Chen: warmers sound smart. who owns the warmers? Redwood or Oakridge?
[04:16] Priya Shah: Redwood can provide a warming runbook and optionally run the warmers during the pilot as part of the managed onboarding phase
[04:26] [04:26] Jordan Lee: quick Q: how does the VPC private deployment affect latency vs hosted? we've heard private planes add hops
[04:36] Priya Shah: VPC adds minimal network overhead, usually under 10-15 ms if peered regionally; the big delta is the control plane handoffs if you're running a private control plane on-prem, that can add overhead if not colocated with GPUs
[04:52] Samir Patel: and on security, finance flagged PCI adjacency - so SOC2 plus KMS integration is required, we need network diagrams and key custody notes
[05:04] Alex Mercer: yes we'll share SOC2 docs and a network diagram; Redwood supports KMS and HSM integrations, we can also confirm audit log retention windows
[05:12] Maya Chen: okay thanks. on the cost model you mentioned scenarios, can you walk through one?
[05:20] Alex Mercer: sure - quick numbers: hosted baseline month $45k; during 3x promo that can spike to $120k; dedicated medium commit reduces baseline to $30k with a 12-month commit and caps promo to approx $55k with autoscale bursts, those are ballpark
[05:40] Jordan Lee: that's a big difference. what's the minimum commit size we should consider?
[05:46] Priya Shah: from the sims, minimum useful commit to materially reduce spike risk is roughly equal to 2x baseline peak; anything smaller yields limited insurance
[05:56] Samir Patel: also curious about throttling behavior - what's Redwood's behavior when capacity saturates? do we queue, reject, or fallback to smaller variant?
[06:06] Alex Mercer: by default we use smart routing: prefer canary smaller variant only for low-priority routes, for critical routes we will return a soft-fail or queue depending on policy; we can configure fast-fail to avoid user impact, and an automatic rollback if quality degrades
[06:24] Maya Chen: we prefer predictable slowdowns over silent quality drops. better to degrade with a visible UX message than silently change model behavior
[06:36] Priya Shah: agreed. we'll show how to set an explicit fallback policy and route-level SLO bindings in the console during the sizing workshop
[06:48] [06:48] Speaker 2: (background noise)
[06:56] Alex Mercer: ok moving on, Priya can you describe the benchmark plan?
[07:02] Priya Shah: sure. we'll run a 24-hour continuous stress benchmark against a staging clone of your checkout pipeline. We'll emulate traffic profiles (burst windows included), monitor P50/P95/P99, GPU utilization, batching stats, KV hit rates, and model swap events. We'll produce a spreadsheet with cost-per-1000-requests at different commit levels
[07:26] Samir Patel: will the benchmark use exact customer data? we need to keep PCI boundaries intact
[07:32] Priya Shah: no customer data. we'll use synthetic payloads that match token distribution and lengths. also we'll obfuscate any patterns you need kept private
[07:42] Maya Chen: timeline?
[07:44] Priya Shah: start as soon as we get traffic profile and access to a staging API endpoint — estimate results in 5 business days after kickoff, so target 2026-06-11 for results
[07:56] Alex Mercer: I'll send the deck + cost spreadsheet after this call. Priya will own the benchmark. Samir you'll send the profile
[08:06] Jordan Lee: regarding observability, can we get token-level cost breakdowns and per-route latency dashboards?
[08:14] Priya Shah: yes, Redwood Console provides token-level cost and latency breakdown; we'll set up the route dashboards and give read-only access to your FinOps team
[08:25] Samir Patel: perfect. any thoughts on quantization and quality tradeoffs? we could look at int8 for non-critical endpoints
[08:34] Priya Shah: int8 looks promising for embeddings and some generation models; we'd do A/B tests on a small subset first to validate no regression on accuracy and fraud-detection heuristics
[08:46] Maya Chen: ok. go-to-market roadmap: we want to be ready for the holiday promo in November, pilot in July/August seems fair?
[08:56] Alex Mercer: yes pilot in July, production by October gives time for iterative tuning and a dry-run before November. commit start could be Sep or Oct depending on results
[09:08] Jordan Lee: about SLAs and penalties, finance will ask for an uptime commitment during peak windows, can Redwood provide time-bound SLOs?
[09:16] Alex Mercer: for Dedicated we can offer SLA-backed latency targets for pinned model routes with an enterprise contract; exact penalty terms to be captured in the contract negotiation
[09:26] Samir Patel: quick note — a competitor mentioned they've offloaded some traffic to a smaller endpoint to keep latency low, wondering if Redwood has similar route-level splitting
[09:36] Priya Shah: yes route-level splitting is supported, and we can do rules by path, user-agent, or feature flag. we'll show a sample routing policy in the workshop
[09:48] Maya Chen: great. on security docs, can you include KMS rotation frequency and HSM vendor details?
[09:56] Alex Mercer: yes we'll include KMS rotation notes, HSM integration options and contact for security review
[10:04] [10:04] Speaker 1: (keyboard clack)
[10:12] Alex Mercer: ok let's close with agreed next steps and owners
[10:16] Maya Chen: recap — benchmark by Redwood, traffic profile from Oakridge, cost model and docs from Alex, schedule workshop, share SOC2 and network diagram
[10:28] Priya Shah: I'll put the benchmark runbook and the templates in a shared folder, and run the test when Samir gives the staging endpoint
[10:36] Samir Patel: I'll send the profile by Monday EOD
[10:40] Jordan Lee: I'll loop in infra team and set up a staging endpoint, we might need a small NAT rule for the warmers
[10:48] Alex Mercer: perfect. any last questions?
[10:52] Maya Chen: none here, thanks everyone
[10:56] Alex Mercer: thanks all, we'll follow up with calendar invites for the workshop; end of call
